architecture.mechanism: Exploit electrokinetic surface potential modulation to repel biofilm/scale nuclei + enhance turbulent mixing to sweep away incipient deposits.
architecture.intervention: Apply a pulsed, low-current cathodic protection current combined with a superhydrophilic nanostructured coating on plate channels, plus controlled flow perturbation via optimized chevron plate geometry retrofits.
architecture.expected_effect: Maintain HTC >2500 W/m²K; pressure drop increase <10% over 12 months; biofilm coverage <5%.
architecture.falsification_test: Run 12-month accelerated fouling test with/without the coating/current; measure HTC decay and pressure drop; if HTC drops >15% or PdP increases >20% in 6 months, falsified.

preserved_objections.basis: Cathodic protection raises local pH via oxygen reduction, promoting CaCO3 scaling, and superhydrophilic surfaces increase surface energy, enhancing biofilm adhesion; the claimed electrokinetic repulsion is contradicted by these known effects.
The hard constraint requires 12 months between cleanings, but the testable prediction only checks 6 months; also, retrofitting chevron geometry violates existing plate constraints.

None of the cited papers address electrokinetic surface potential modulation or cathodic protection; the nano-silica coating paper is for cooling towers, not plate heat exchangers, and does not support the combined mechanism.
Applying electrical current to individual plates in an assembled PHE is impractical and risks galvanic corrosion; nanostructured coating on internal channels is
